children.author: jlev1
children.text:
It’s the nature of mathematical ideas and methods that they are reducible to their component parts, so if you really want to, you can nearly always claim that something is just recombining existing knowledge. Motivated reasoning, from people dead-set on embellishing or downplaying a result, is hard to avoid here, so all you can really do is make an earnest and sincere judgment call based on the fine details of the mathematics.

For example, it is my opinion that the Jacobian conjecture counterexample was, in retrospect, easy and classical and hiding in plain sight, and that it’s a bit embarrassing we didn't find it decades ago. (I wrote about the construction on my blog btw!) In contrast, the Unit Distance Conjecture counterexample seemed to me to use a stroke of genius by applying techniques from class field theory to approach what seemed like a problem in discrete geometry and combinatorics. It’s a neat, if annoying, feature of math that once we find a long-sought solution to an open problem, we reserve the right to retrospectively change our mind about the value of the problem if the solution turns out too easy or uninteresting. We just have to try to be fair and honest about it (the word “just” is doing some heavy lifting in this sentence).

Anyway, I don’t think “brute force recombination” is likely to be meaningfully the case here with GRH, though we won’t know for sure until the proof has been simplified and distilled. Alpöge’s sketch in his announcement yesterday included (IIRC) connections to the function field setting and new ideas about Fourier analysis.

The problem we need to solve is that building a Lean project allows for arbitrary code execution, just like many other programming languages. Thus, building a Lean project might interfere with your proof checking infrastructure and fool it into accepting an incorrect proof.

"Building" a Lean project actually consists of two steps that can be separated: compiling the high-level Lean document to the simple expression format of the Lean kernel (this part is called "elaboration") and then checking that this expression consistutes a valid proof of the claimed statement (this part is called "kernel checking"). Only the first part potentially involves arbitrary code execution.

Lean ships with a component called `lake comparator` [1]. It works like this: a trusted challenge (formal statement) and the potential proof are elaborated separately in sandboxed environments so that code execution during the build of the proof cannot interfere with the checker or the trusted statement. Then the statement and proof are both exported into a simple JSON-format [2] that represents the relevant terms in the expression format of the Lean kernel, and then the checkers check this JSON.

If this process succeeds, then you know that you definitely have a proof of the relevant statement, with the JSON as a witness of the proof.

[1]: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/... [2]: https://github.com/leanprover/lean4export

> There are still a few ways that the proof might be incorrect

I hear there's a teapot kicking around between us and Mars, too

There are still a few ways that the proof might be incorrect. Of these, the most likely is that the proof was generated by a misaligned AI system that found and intentionally exploited a lean bug in order to fool its human evaluators (i.e. shades of the HuggingFace attack). I personally don't think this is very likely, but you'd have to understand a bit more about the agent systems used in generating the proof to come up with a more informed estimate.

Another possibility is that an aligned system came up with a plausible but incorrect idea along the way, and simultaneously stumbled across a lean bug that led to an incorrect verification of this idea. I'd put the likelihood here as vanishingly small due to the requirement of serendipitous factors, but it's nonzero.

You could also ask whether an aligned AI system could "p-hack" its way into finding a serendipitous lean bug by trying a large number of approaches. I think this is also vanishingly unlikely because the AI system is trained on and therefore "thinking in" natural language, and presumably only translating results into lean after it believes them to be correct.

And of course there's the possibility that the lean proof isn't faithful to the natural language description we've been given, but that is ruled out in this case due to the use of the canonical problem statement in mathlib. Otherwise, this would certainly seem like the most likely way the proof could be incorrect.

As a result, whatever accrues to these endeavors as a result of "value" will go more towards the person with those extra resources, and cause a rich-get-richer spiral.

This is just a performance issue. In theory, the Lean kernel could be written in Lean.

These independent kernels do not prove their own consistency -- rather, their function is to act as slower but more idiomatic/simpler implementations of Lean's meta-theory. It doesn't matter that they don't correspond 1:1 with Lean's official kernel at either a theoretical or an implementation level, because the independent kernels are not for proving Lean correct -- they're for auditing complex proofs, in a simpler system.

What is particularly interesting is that then these independent kernels are "proven correct"! This notion of correctness is specifically that con-leche (et al) will only accept theorems that are also correct with regards to a particular model of set theory, with membership / extensionality / other standard ZF axioms, and an infinite hierarchy of universes. This is (vaguely speaking) a set-theoretic model of Lean. It is here that Gödel's incompleteness theorems come into play. Lean indeed cannot verify that this set-theoretic model is "correct": what it can verify, however, is that the type-theoretic machinery is correct with respect to the set-theoretic machinery. This removes the possibility of an invalid proof slipping by by way Lean's comparator (which can run alternative kernels) by way of an implementation bug.

It leaves the possibility that Lean's metatheory is inconsistent. This is quite unlikely. The foundations of mathematics have been well-studied, and Lean builds directly on the huge amount of work that has been done, particularly by the Coq community, in figuring out what is and isn't consistent. The Coq theorem prover was really developed in conjunction with modern type theory... Lean came in after a lot of meta-theoretic issues had been ironed out, thanks to them.

The main issue is on how you define a "Type". There are two different logics here;

1) Classical Logic/Set Theory (this is the one you are talking about). Here Type = Set of values defined by membership rules (extensional/intensional).

2) Intuitionistic Constructive Logic/Type Theory (this is what is preferred for proof assistants). Here Type = Set of constructive (often inductive) proofs where the proof itself is the value.

As an example, think of defining the Type "Even_t"; under (1) it can be a predicate "x % 2 == 0", while under (2) it is defined inductively as "0 is Even_t; if construct(n) is Even_t so is construct(n+2)".

Notice that in the latter case a Type maps nicely into the idea of "a computation" and the fact that the very act of generation of one of its inhabitants constitutes "the proof" that the value has that property!

Whereas in Set theory Types are just subsets. But because you can mix anything into a set, an untyped term can be nonsense and will only get caught when you try to use it. Type Theory disallows it by construction.

This leads to the "Curry-Howard Correspondence" so you get a mapping between logic and type theory concepts - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspon...

This idea of "Typing" can further be extended (with additions of Dependent Types etc.) giving a complex matrix of powerful Type Theories represented by what is known as "Lambda Cube" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_cube) and their implementations in proof assistants eg. Calculus of Constructions (CoC), Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC) etc.

Finally, note that not all proof assistants use constructive logic, several use straight ZFC/HOL. Amongst those that use constructive logic it is usually only the kernel (containing the Type System) which models it while the rest of the system still uses classical logic.

PS: See also the previous discussion Why is dependent type theory more suitable than set theory for proof assistants? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25167468

I am sure you will get some more detailed answers; I am a bit lazy today; so I will give you the very high level / informal version of the answer (Edit from the future: It grew longer than expected, whelp :D):

Gödel's two incompleteness theorems basically amount to "As soon as your system can do a ridicolously little amount of things, then either of two things is true in this system: 1) You can express facts in your system that you cannot prove within your system or 2) your system claims that some false statement is true."

Now, because 2) is way way worse than 1), you design your systems so that you are firmly in the 1) camp - that way, we gain full confidence in the results our systems proofs, and the price we pay is that our system is less powerfull than it could be.

With Lean, it's similar. The foundation of Lean comes from type theory. There, we do something that is familar to above: We restrict our power (i.e. "which Lean statements do get verified by lean?", and we gain absolute confidence in its proofs (ignoring implementation errors, hardware limitations etc. for now). Intuitively: We have to work harder to satisfy the typechecker/prover, but when it is satisfied, then we have confidence in it.

-------------- Deeper down the rabbit hole

You might have noticed that I seem to muddle the waters a bit with programs, proofs, types and so on... There is a deep reason behind it! In a very strong sense, programs = types = proofs... So, here is how it is all connected (including the RH):

- Lean is a programming language (like Haskell, Rust, ... There is nothing stopping you from writing a server in Lean and deploying that binary somewhere in the cloud. Regarding developer experience, you could think of it like a modern Haskell without lazy evaluation and without its historical warts)

- programs can be tied to types: We first check if the whole program as such has a type ("do all of its parts fit together in a strictly defined way?"). Only if it does, we proceed (and for example, run it). If it does not, then the compiler declares "this program is not good! here is a type error!". Now, here is the price hat Gödel proved we cannot avoid (if we want to trust the typechecker): There are programs that don't type check, but behave perfectly fine at runtime. (That's the "we limit our power" part - those are perfectly good programs where the compiler throws their hand in the air and gives up!)

- Enter the third puzzle piece: proofs and the Riemann Hypothesis: turns out, we can think of types as theorems, and a successful type check as a correct proof! And the RH is a hypothesis we would like to prove...

- So here is how it all ties together: RH is written so that it can be used as a type, in the Lean programming language. The "main program" is basically just another ordinary function with some input types, and returns the type version of the RH being true. Because the function needs an implementation, we are forced to implement that function body - which are many small functions that correspond to mathematical theorems/lemmas if you look at it with the proof glasses on. From the programming pov, it is just functions that call functions that call functions and so on. And from the typechecking point of view; we compose a bunch of functions and check whether input types and output types match up.

Finally, the payoff: *If that program typechecks, then we know RH is true*, which is what just happened!

(PS: The same principle is behind the computational proof of the four-color-theorem. The proof of the four color theorem is "simply" a program that typechecks, where the final type happens to correspond to "can we color any planar graph with at most 4 colors?")

In a parliamentary system such as the UK, Canada or Australia, this tends to be less of an issue – the executive government is under the direct control of the legislature, so if the Attorney-General or Solicitor-General submits a brief arguing for a particular interpretation of legislation, the current legislative majority (which might not necessarily be the majority which enacted that legislation to begin with) can be understood as effectively endorsing it.

In a presidential system such as the US, where there is a strong separation between the executive and legislative branches, legislator amicus briefs make somewhat more sense – and members of US Congress submitting amicus briefs to appellate courts actually does happen reasonably frequently; however, the courts tend not to put much weight on them.

But what has always baffled me, AFAIK, the original legislators don't file Amicus Briefs when the meaning of laws are argued in court. I mean in situations where the original legislator is still alive and of good mind, why doesn't the Judge just ask them what the spirt of the law is?

Laws are supposed to be applied (by judges, bureaucrats, etc) with discretion and common sense, not mechanically. Of course, that can sometimes result in injustices – exceptions being made for some people not others for reasons of political or societal biases – but it also avoids a lot of injustices: thoughtless/mechanical application of the law can result in outcomes which the legislator never intended and few would consider just or fair or reasonable.

I think, if we actually started applying laws in such a mechanical way, we'd end up with laws changing a lot more frequently, and with a lot more special cases written in to them – now, if applying a law in a certain situation seems unreasonable, judges will often choose not to apply it; with mechanical application, they'd have no choice, and then the people negatively impacted would lobby the legislature for a change in the legal text, and they'd probably get it. It could also see increased use of executive clemency (the power of pardon), or its legislative equivalent (legislation retroactively declaring certain convictions null and void).

One indeed might wonder whether the "human-led" efforts of Mathlib are worthwhile. First, it must be noted that Mathlib serves two purposes -- to be a reusable and robust collection of formally-verified mathematical statements, but also to be a learning resource for students of mathematics without access to the rigour that an academic education provides. It is for this reason that the human nature of mathematical exposition is deeply important. In mathematics, a proof is more than a blackbox -- it is (or was) the way in which you explain mathematics.

(I consider "proof" somewhat unfortunate terminology for these slop nukes, as such. I think the term "certificate" is better. 17 million lines of Lean does not pragmatically convey anything other than whether a statement is true or false. It may be easier communication, but it is deeply, deeply, inefficient communication.)

The first goal of Mathlib is indeed not in conflict with slop nukes, however. One of the projects of the Lean FRO (or just a Lean FRO member? unclear to me how endorsed it is) is a version of Mathlib that fully embraces slop: https://taucetiproject.org/. However, there's really no bottleneck there. If there is any non-novel mathematics in Anthropic's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that is not already in Tau Ceti, it is simply because they have not bothered yet. Auto-formalization works, at scale, very well, as harmful to the human as it might be.

The proof is written in a programming language called Lean. Very roughly, Lean is set up so that proofs are functions and theorems are types in this language. Verifying that the proof is correct essentially amounts to compiling the program and confirming that it doesn't have any type errors. Several people have compiled the program successfully, so we believe it's correct.

The biggest concern that people have is that there might be a bug in the type checker that the proof is exploiting. But a) it's been compiled with multiple independently-implemented compilers, which are are unlikely to have the same bugs, and b) some of those compilers have themselves been proven to contain no bugs. So, it is exceedingly likely that the proof is legitimate.

Now, whether we can understand the proof is an open question...

A party interested in proving me wrong wheels in a machine draped in a cloth. They reach under the cloth to turn it on. It whirs and a short while later ejects a brass spring.

No matter what kind of machine is under the cloth, my theory has been proven false. I should reveal the machine under the cloth only if I'm interested in knowing how the machine works, but either way there is clearly a machine that can produce brass springs.
